problem:
A customer of Meridian Bank buys a laptop for EUR 1,200 at Northgate Retail using a Meridian credit card. The terminal shows the payment as approved, the customer leaves with the laptop, and Northgate expects the funds in its account. Two days later, Northgate's finance team cannot match the sale to a settlement, and the customer sees a pending authorisation on the card statement but no completed charge.

The confusion comes from treating authorisation, clearing, billing and settlement as one event. Authorisation only reserves funds and checks the card. Clearing moves the transaction record to the scheme and the issuer. Settlement moves the money. Billing shows the charge to the cardholder. The learner must trace the transaction through each touchpoint and explain where it can stall, what each party sees, and how a dispute would be handled.
solution:
Teach the card flow as four distinct stages with different owners and different evidence. Authorisation happens in seconds: the terminal sends the card and transaction details to the acquirer, the scheme routes them to the issuer, and the issuer checks the card status, the available credit and fraud rules, then approves or declines and places a hold on the funds. The authorisation code is the key reference for everything that follows.

Clearing happens later, usually in batches. The merchant submits the approved transaction, the acquirer sends a clearing record through the scheme, and the issuer receives it and matches it to the authorisation. Settlement then moves the money: the issuer pays the scheme, the scheme pays the acquirer, and the acquirer credits the merchant, each less any agreed fees. Billing shows the completed charge on the cardholder statement once clearing has matched.

When a transaction is missing from settlement, trace it by authorisation code, transaction reference and batch ID across the merchant, acquirer, scheme and issuer records. A duplicate clearing record must be deduplicated by its message identity so it creates no second charge. A delayed clearing acknowledgement must be handled by holding the transaction in an awaiting-clearing state, never by resubmitting it blindly. Disputes follow a separate path: the cardholder raises the dispute, the issuer investigates with the merchant evidence, and the outcome is a chargeback or a rejection of the dispute, each with its own accounting treatment.

decision.question: A EUR 1,200 card purchase shows as approved at the terminal, but two days later the merchant cannot match the sale to a settlement and the cardholder sees only a pending authorisation. What is the most likely situation and the right first step?

options.label: A
options.detail: The payment failed, so the merchant should ask the customer to pay again.

options.label: B
options.detail: Authorisation succeeded but clearing or settlement has not yet completed or reconciled, so trace the transaction by its authorisation code and transaction reference through the acquirer, scheme and issuer records before acting.

options.label: C
options.detail: The merchant should write off the sale.

options.label: D
options.detail: The cardholder should be charged again by the issuer.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because an approved authorisation is only the first stage. Clearing and settlement follow, and a mismatch is usually a timing or reconciliation break, not proof of failure. Option A risks double charging the customer. Option D duplicates the charge. Option C gives up a valid sale without evidence.

steps.title: Presents the card at the Northgate terminal for EUR 1,200
Sends the authorisation request through the card scheme to the issuer
Checks the card, available credit and fraud rules, approves the transaction and places a hold
Completes the sale and submits the transaction in the daily clearing batch
Routes the clearing record to the issuer and calculates settlement
Matches the clearing record to the authorisation and confirms the charge
Moves funds from issuer to scheme to acquirer, less agreed fees
Credit the merchant account and show the completed charge on the cardholder statement

happy: Authorisation is approved in seconds with an authorisation code. The transaction clears in the daily batch, settlement completes for the expected net amount, the merchant is credited, and the cardholder statement shows the completed EUR 1,200 charge with the merchant name. The authorisation hold is replaced by the completed charge.

negative.title: Clearing acknowledgement delayed
negative.detail: The clearing record is submitted but no acknowledgement arrives in the expected window. Hold the transaction in an awaiting-clearing state, correlate by transaction reference, and investigate without blind resubmission.

negative.title: Settlement amount differs
negative.detail: The settlement report shows a different amount from the submitted sale. Classify the difference as fees, partial settlement or error, reconcile at the correct level, and post adjustments only under approved rules.

negative.title: Duplicate clearing record
negative.detail: The same clearing record arrives twice. Deduplicate by message and transaction identity, make clearing handling idempotent, and ensure no second charge or second merchant credit is created.

negative.title: Cardholder dispute
negative.detail: The cardholder disputes the charge after the statement arrives. Raise a dispute case with the authorisation code, clearing evidence and merchant records, follow the scheme dispute process, and post any chargeback as a separate controlled transaction.

technical: Use the authorisation code, transaction reference, card reference and batch ID as the stable tracing keys across merchant, acquirer, scheme and issuer. Keep authorisation, clearing and settlement as separate states with explicit transitions, and never treat an authorisation as proof of settlement. Make clearing and status handling idempotent by message identity so duplicate records create no second effect. Record the authorisation hold, its expiry, the cleared amount, fees and the settlement amount as separate data items. Validate card data handling, tokenisation and masking rules, and keep the full transaction trail for dispute and audit purposes. Reconcile authorisations against clearing records and clearing records against settlement reports daily.

accounting: Authorisation places a hold on the cardholder's available credit without posting a completed charge. Clearing converts the hold into a posted charge: debit the cardholder account and credit the scheme settlement account. Settlement credits the merchant account for the net amount after fees, and fees are recorded as separate income lines. A duplicate clearing record must not create a second charge. A chargeback debits the merchant and credits the cardholder as a separate controlled transaction with its own reference. Operations reconciles authorisations to clearing records and clearing records to settlement reports daily, and unmatched items sit on a worklist with an owner and a service level.

questions.question: What does a card authorisation do?
options: It checks the card and reserves funds, but it does not by itself settle the payment.
questions.explanation: Authorisation approves and holds funds. Clearing and settlement follow as separate stages.

questions.question: Why might a merchant not see a settlement two days after an approved sale?
options: Clearing or settlement may still be in progress, or the settlement may not have reconciled to the sale.
questions.explanation: Authorisation, clearing and settlement run on different cycles, and a reconciliation break can also delay matching.

questions.question: The same clearing record arrives twice. What must happen?
options: Deduplicate by message identity so only one charge and one merchant credit occur.
questions.explanation: Idempotent clearing handling ensures duplicate delivery has no second financial effect.

questions.question: A cardholder disputes a completed charge. What is the correct handling?
options: Raise a dispute case with authorisation, clearing and merchant evidence, follow the scheme process, and post any chargeback as a separate controlled transaction.
Ask the merchant to pay the cardholder directly.
questions.explanation: Disputes follow a defined scheme process with evidence, and a chargeback is a separate transaction with its own reference.
